_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-29 00:41:55Z)**_

Issue #93 in the CSCI-435-SE/cal.diy repo is "Add long-press to start drag on touch devices in the weekly availability grid." It's assigned to you and tagged `enhancement` and `effort:medium`.

## The problem

Issue #70 added drag-to-select to the weekly availability grid. On touch screens, the day cells use `touch-none` (`touch-action: none`), so the browser doesn't scroll while you drag. As a result, any finger that lands on a cell starts a selection right away.

On a phone the grid fills most of the screen. A user who tries to scroll the page or the grid ends up selecting or deselecting time slots by accident. Scrolling only works if you drag on the hour-label column or the day header, and most users won't find that.

## The fix: long-press to drag (like Google Calendar mobile)

| Input | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Touch swipe | Scrolls normally, no selection |
| Touch press-and-hold (~350ms, no movement) | Starting cell highlights, then dragging selects or deselects exactly as in #70 (same mode rule, stays in one column, auto-scrolls near edges) |
| Mouse / pen | Unchanged, drag starts immediately |

## Acceptance criteria
1. A quick swipe that starts on a cell scrolls and never changes the selection.
2. Hold for ~350ms, then drag: same select/deselect behavior as #70, including auto-scroll.
3. Once a long-press drag starts, the page and grid don't scroll under the finger (except the grid's own edge auto-scroll).
4. A long press doesn't open the context menu, the iOS callout, or a text selection.
5. Mouse behavior is unchanged.
6. Tests cover the hold threshold, cancelling on movement, and mouse versus touch.

## Implementation plan from the issue
- **Hook (`packages/features/schedules/hooks/useWeeklyGridDrag.ts`):** on a touch `pointerdown`, start a timer instead of a drag. Cancel it if the finger moves more than ~8px or if a `pointercancel` fires (the browser has taken over scrolling).
- **Blocking scroll once dragging:** add a native `touchmove` listener with `{ passive: false }` that calls `preventDefault()`. React's touch handlers are passive, so they can't do this.
- **Grid (`packages/features/schedules/components/WeeklyAvailabilityGrid.tsx`):** on line 125, change `touch-none` to `touch-pan-y`. Add `onContextMenu={e => e.preventDefault()}` and `-webkit-touch-callout: none`.
- **Tests:** use Vitest fake timers in `useWeeklyGridDrag.test.tsx`. Real scrolling can't be simulated in jsdom, so check it by hand on a phone or with Chrome DevTools touch emulation.

**Existing tests will break:** `WeeklyAvailabilityGrid.test.tsx` checks for `touch-none` on lines 96 and 126–127, so those assertions need to be updated.

## Scope
- **Related to #71 (grid/list toggle):** users can't see the grid until #71 lands, so this is a usability fix before release rather than an urgent bug.
- **Out of scope:** keyboard selection and any change to mouse behavior.
- **Alternatives the issue rejected:** an "Edit" toggle (adds an extra tap and UI state), two-finger scroll (hard to discover), and a movement-direction threshold (conflicts with vertical drags).

Your `feat/issue-93` branch has no commits beyond `main` yet. Starting with the hook logic and its tests makes sense, since the grid changes are small.

**Source**
1. **`hooks/useWeeklyGridDrag.ts`**: most of the work goes here.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-29 00:55:46Z)**_

Partly. Changing the dimensions alone won't test this issue, because the code checks the input type, not the screen size.

**Why size isn't enough:** the long-press logic only runs when `pointerType === "touch"`. If you just resize the window, you're still clicking with a mouse, so the drag starts immediately as it does today. The grid looks like a phone layout, but you're testing mouse behavior.

**How to set up touch emulation in Chrome DevTools:**
1. Open DevTools and turn on the Device Toolbar (Ctrl+Shift+M).
2. Pick a device preset, such as iPhone 14 or Pixel 7. Presets turn on touch emulation, and the cursor changes to a gray circle. If you use "Responsive" instead, set the device type to **Mobile**, which also enables touch.
3. Reload the page after switching, since some touch detection only happens on load.
4. To confirm, run `matchMedia("(pointer: coarse)").matches` in the console. It should return `true`.

**What you can check this way:**
- A quick swipe on a cell scrolls without selecting.
- Holding ~350ms, then dragging, selects or deselects and auto-scrolls near the edges.
- Moving the finger before the hold finishes cancels the drag.
- The page doesn't scroll under your finger once a drag has started.
- With the Device Toolbar off, the mouse behaves exactly as before.

**Limits of emulation:**
- The iOS callout (`-webkit-touch-callout`) and real Safari scrolling only show up on an actual iPhone. If you can, open your local dev server on a phone on the same Wi-Fi network.
- Emulated scroll momentum isn't quite like a real finger, so treat it as a close approximation.

You'll also still need to temporarily set `availabilityView="grid"` (don't commit it) to see the grid at all, since #71's toggle isn't in `main`.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-29 01:02:34Z)**_

Almost all of the change goes in `hooks/useWeeklyGridDrag.ts`. The grid component only needs a one-line class change. Two things in the current code make this simpler:

- The pointer handlers are attached to the row container (`rowsRef`, `WeeklyAvailabilityGrid.tsx` line 93), not to each cell. So the hook already has one element where it can attach a native `touchmove` listener.
- While a drag is active, the hook already shows a preview of the selection change. When the hold finishes and the drag starts, the starting cell changes color immediately, so you don't need extra highlight code.

## What happens now vs. after

**Now (`onPointerDown`, line 128):** every pointer type starts a drag immediately. The cell's `touch-none` class stops the browser from scrolling.

**After:**
- **Mouse or pen:** follows the same code path as today.
- **Touch, `pointerdown`:** records the start position and starts a 350ms timer. It doesn't start the drag, call `preventDefault`, or capture the pointer yet.
- **Touch, `pointermove` before the timer fires:** if the finger has moved more than 8px, cancels the timer. With the new `touch-pan-y` class, the browser scrolls normally.
- **Touch, browser starts scrolling:** the browser fires `pointercancel`, which cancels the timer.
- **Touch, timer fires:** starts the drag, using the same function the mouse uses.
- **Touch, `touchmove` while dragging:** a native listener calls `preventDefault()` so the page doesn't scroll.
- **`pointerup` before the timer fires:** cancels the timer and changes nothing.

## Changes to the hook

1. **Pull the start logic into a shared function.** Move lines 136–144 into a `startDrag(position, clientY, element, pointerId)` function that both paths call. That's what keeps the mouse behavior identical.
2. **Add a ref for the pending hold:**
   ```ts
   const pendingHoldRef = useRef<{ timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>; x: number; y: number } | null>(null);
   ```
   Also add a `cancelHold()` function that clears the timer.
3. **Branch in `onPointerDown`:**
   ```ts
   if (event.pointerType !== "touch") { startDrag(...); return; }
   const { clientX, clientY, pointerId, currentTarget } = event; // capture now, the event is reused
   pendingHoldRef.current = {
     x: clientX, y: clientY,
     timer: setTimeout(() => { pendingHoldRef.current = null; startDrag(position, clientY, currentTarget, pointerId); }, LONG_PRESS_MS),
   };
   ```
   You have to copy those values out of the event before the timer runs, because React reuses event objects. `setPointerCapture` must happen inside the timer, not on press, or capturing could interfere with scrolling.
4. **`onPointerMove`:** if a hold is pending and the finger has moved more than `LONG_PRESS_MOVE_TOLERANCE_PX` (8), cancel it. Otherwise, keep the existing drag-following code.
5. **`onPointerUp` and `onPointerCancel`:** call `cancelHold()` first, then do what they do now.
6. **Add a native `touchmove` blocker in a `useEffect`:**
   ```ts
   useEffect(() => {
     const rows = rowsRef.current;
     if (!rows) return;
     const block = (e: TouchEvent) => { if (dragRef.current) e.preventDefault(); };
     rows.addEventListener("touchmove", block, { passive: false });
     return () => rows.removeEventListener("touchmove", block);
   }, [rowsRef]);
   ```
   This has to be a native listener because React registers its touch listeners as passive, and passive listeners can't call `preventDefault`.
7. **Clear the timer on unmount** in the same cleanup, so an old timer can't fire later.
8. **Add `onContextMenu: (e) => e.preventDefault()` to the returned `handlers`.** The grid already spreads `handlers` onto the rows, so it picks this up automatically.

## Changes to the grid component

Only line 125 changes:
```ts
isEditable && "cursor-pointer touch-pan-y [-webkit-touch-callout:none]"
```
Also update the comment above it, since it describes the old reason for `touch-none`.

## One behavior change to decide on

Right now a quick **tap** on a cell toggles that one slot, because the drag starts and ends on the same cell. With long-press, a quick touch tap does nothing. That's consistent with acceptance criterion 1 (a quick touch shouldn't change the selection), and it's how Google Calendar behaves. Still, it's worth mentioning in your PR description, or confirming with your team, so nobody reports it as a bug.

If you want, I can write the hook changes and the fake-timer tests next. I'll leave the commits to you.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-29 01:21:24Z)**_

No, laptops keep tap-to-toggle. The long-press logic switches on input type (`event.pointerType`), not on screen size or device, so only finger input changes.

| Input | `pointerType` | Behavior after the change |
|---|---|---|
| Laptop trackpad | `"mouse"` | Same as today: a click toggles, a drag selects right away |
| Mouse | `"mouse"` | Same as today |
| Stylus or Apple Pencil | `"pen"` | Same as today |
| Finger on a phone or tablet | `"touch"` | Long-press to drag, and a quick tap does nothing |

So the tap change is phone-only in practice, which is what you want.

**One exception:** touchscreen laptops, like a Surface or many Windows 2-in-1s. If someone touches the screen with a finger, that counts as `"touch"` and gets the long-press behavior. Their trackpad and mouse still work as they do today. That's probably correct: a finger on the screen has the same accidental-scroll problem as on a phone. It's still worth one line in your PR so reviewers know it's intentional.

**If you want to keep tap-to-toggle on phones too:** in `onPointerUp`, if a hold is still pending (the finger lifted before 350ms without moving more than 8px), toggle that one cell. A tap would toggle, a swipe would still scroll, and a hold would still drag, so criterion 1 is still met. The downside is that a tap made while trying to stop a scroll could toggle a cell by accident. I'd still go with "a tap does nothing," like Google Calendar, but either option meets the acceptance criteria.

I re-read `useWeeklyGridDrag.ts`, `WeeklyAvailabilityGrid.tsx`, both test files, and how `AvailabilitySettings.tsx` wires up the grid. I haven't changed any files. The design holds up with a few corrections: the `touch-action` approach is a standard pattern, but the earlier plan missed four things.

- **Taps:** it treated "a quick tap does nothing" as required. Issue #93 doesn't require that, and a tap can keep toggling a cell.
- **Multiple fingers:** a second finger can take over or end a drag. That's a gap in the current code too.
- **Stale values:** two values would be read late in the timer instead of at the moment of the press.
- **Android:** it didn't flag that Android's own long-press handling could interfere.

## 1. Can `pan-y` plus a non-passive `touchmove` listener reliably start a drag after 350ms?

Yes. This is the same approach react-beautiful-dnd and dnd-kit use for touch delays.

**Who controls the gesture:**
- With `touch-action: pan-y`, the browser doesn't decide to scroll on press. It waits until the finger moves past its own small movement threshold.
- Before it scrolls, the browser has to send a `touchmove` that the page can cancel, and it waits for non-passive listeners to finish.
- If that `touchmove` is cancelled, the browser never starts scrolling, so it never fires `pointercancel`, and pointer events keep arriving.
- Because the listener runs before the browser decides, there's no race.

**`pointercancel`:**
- If the finger moves before 350ms, the browser takes over scrolling and fires `pointercancel`, which cancels the hold. That's what criterion 1 needs.
- After a drag has started, `pointercancel` only happens if something outside our control interrupts. Examples are an OS gesture or an Android long-press, covered under risks. The existing `onPointerCancel` already discards the preview without saving. If that happens, the drag is lost but the user's availability isn't changed by accident.

**Where the listener goes:** on the rows element (`rowsRef`). Touch events always target the element the finger first landed on and bubble up from there. So the listener on rows gets every `touchmove`, even when the finger moves into the header.

**Drag mode and highlight:** the drag mode is worked out on press and stored with the pending hold, so the timer doesn't need to read `value` later. The "drag started" highlight comes from the existing preview, so no new rendering code is needed.

## 2. Mouse and pen stay exactly the same

- `onPointerDown` branches first: anything that isn't `"touch"` calls a `startDrag()` function containing exactly what lines 136–144 do today. That includes `preventDefault`, pointer capture, and the drag-state setup.
- `onPointerMove`, `onPointerUp`, auto-scroll and the preview don't change for mouse.
- The new `touchmove` listener only acts during a drag and only receives touch events, so mouse users never reach it.
- All existing hook tests use `pointerType: "mouse"`. They should pass unchanged, and that's how we prove this.

## 3. Taps: not required by #93, and they can stay

**What the issue requires:** criterion 1 is about swipes, and a tap isn't a swipe. Nothing in #93 asks for taps to stop working. #70 has a test, "toggles a single slot on click" (line 168), which shows tap-to-toggle was intended. Removing it on phones would change behavior beyond this issue's scope.

**When a tap toggles:** a touch toggles one cell if all of these hold:
- the finger lifts before 350ms
- it moved 8px or less
- no `pointercancel` fired

It reuses the same commit code with the start and end slot equal, so the result is identical to a mouse click today.

**The one risk: taps that stop a scroll.** When a scroll is still gliding after a swipe, users often tap to stop it. Browsers block the `click` for that tap, but they still fire `pointerdown` and `pointerup`, so the code above would toggle a cell.

**The guard:**
- Add one passive scroll listener on `document` (capture phase), so it catches scrolling of both the grid and the page.
- Store the time of the most recent scroll in a ref.
- A tap only toggles if no scroll happened in the ~100ms before `pointerdown`.

The guard adds about 10 lines. If the team prefers "tap does nothing," drop the guard and the tap logic. Both options meet all six criteria. **I recommend keeping taps with the guard**, but this is the one decision I'd confirm with your team.

## 4. Edge cases

| Case | Handling |
|---|---|
| **Second finger during a hold** | A non-primary `pointerdown` cancels the hold, since it's a multi-finger gesture, not a long press. This check runs before the existing `!isPrimary` early return. |
| **Second finger during a drag** | Store `pointerId` in the existing drag state. Move, up and cancel events with a different `pointerId` are ignored. Today the hook doesn't check `pointerId` at all, so a second finger's `pointermove` would move the selection and its `pointerup` would end the drag. Mouse never shows this because it has one pointer. |
| **Movement tolerance** | During a pending hold, measure distance from the press point. Over 8px cancels the hold. In practice, vertical movement usually triggers the browser's `pointercancel` first; horizontal movement (which `pan-y` doesn't scroll) relies on the 8px check. Also update `pointerYRef` during the hold, so the drag picks up from where the finger actually is. |
| **Early release** | `pointerup` during a pending hold clears the timer, then either toggles one cell (tap rule above) or does nothing. |
| **Unmount** | One `useEffect` cleanup clears the timer and removes the `touchmove` and scroll listeners. Auto-scroll already stops itself on unmount. |
| **Pointer capture fails** | Put `setPointerCapture` in a small try/catch helper and treat failure as harmless. For touch, the browser already captures the pointer to the pressed cell, so events still bubble to rows. For mouse, failure behaves like today in jsdom, where the existing `?.` already allows it to be missing. |
| **Grid becomes read-only mid-hold** | The timer callback checks a ref for the current `onSelectionChange` and does nothing if it's gone. It reads a ref so that a change to the callback doesn't cancel holds. (`AvailabilitySettings` passes a stable `useCallback` either way.) |

## 5. Behavior from #70 that stays the same

**Same column, mode, preview and auto-scroll:** the touch path ends in the same `startDrag()` and uses the same `followPointer` and `useEdgeAutoScroll`, so all of these behave identically for touch and mouse.

**Edge auto-scroll during a touch drag:** it still works. It changes `scrollTop` directly, which the `touchmove` cancellation doesn't block.

## 6. Can the existing hook handle this without much added complexity?

Yes, with no new React state:
- One ref for the pending hold: `{ pointerId, position, mode, x, y, timer }`
- `pointerId` added to the existing drag state
- One ref for the last scroll time, only if taps are kept
- One `useEffect` for the native listeners and timer cleanup
- Two constants: `LONG_PRESS_MS = 350` and `LONG_PRESS_MOVE_TOLERANCE_PX = 8`

`onPointerUp`'s commit logic moves into a `commitDrag(state)` function so taps can reuse it. `onContextMenu` is added to the returned handlers, so the grid picks it up through its existing spread.

**The grid itself:** the line 125 class becomes `touch-pan-y [-webkit-touch-callout:none]`, and the comment above it gets updated.

**Size:** 2 source files and 2 test files, about 200–300 lines. That's within the PR limits.

## 7. Tests

**Hook unit tests (`useWeeklyGridDrag.test.tsx`):** use `vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ["setTimeout", "clearTimeout"] })`. Faking only these two avoids clashing with the test file's own `requestAnimationFrame` mock.

1. Mouse and pen start immediately, with no timer advance needed. The existing tests stay unchanged.
2. Touch: no preview at 349ms, and the start cell is previewed at 350ms.
3. Touch hold, then move: the selection extends, same column only, and saves on release.
4. Touch hold on a selected cell, then move: the drag deselects.
5. Movement over 8px horizontally during the hold: no drag starts, and nothing changes.
6. Movement of 8px or less: the drag still starts.
7. `pointercancel` during the hold: no drag starts afterward.
8. Quick tap: toggles one cell, and `vi.getTimerCount()` returns 0 afterward.
9. Tap within 100ms of a scroll event: nothing changes.
10. Second finger during the hold cancels it. Second finger during a drag: its move and up events are ignored.
11. Unmounting during a hold: no callback fires and no timers remain.
12. `setPointerCapture` throws: the drag still works.
13. A cancelable `touchmove` sent to rows gets `defaultPrevented` only during an active drag, not during a hold or when idle.
14. `contextmenu` gets `defaultPrevented`.
15. Edge auto-scroll works after a touch hold.

**Grid tests (`WeeklyAvailabilityGrid.test.tsx`):** update the `touch-none` assertions on lines 96 and 126–127 to `touch-pan-y` plus the callout class. Also rename the test "prevents … page scrolling on cells," since cells now allow vertical scrolling.

**Browser checks jsdom can't do:**
- **Real phones (required):** iOS Safari and Android Chrome. Swipe on a cell scrolls; hold then drag selects; the page doesn't move during a drag; no menu, callout or text selection; tapping to stop a scroll doesn't toggle a cell.
- **Chrome DevTools touch emulation:** catches most of these, but not the iOS callout or Android's long-press menu.
- **Optional Playwright test:** Chromium can send real touch gestures through the browser's own scroll handling, which would automate the scroll-vs-drag checks. That means adding E2E tests, and the repo rules say to ask before adding or running E2E, so I'd only add it if you want.

## Unresolved risks

1. **Android Chrome long-press (highest):** Chrome's own long-press fires around 400–500ms, after our drag has started. Blocking `contextmenu` should keep the touch going, but I can't confirm Chrome won't send `pointercancel` anyway. If it does, the drag is discarded without saving. That fails safe, but the feature would be broken on Android. Test this on a real device first.
2. **iOS Safari:** the callout, text-selection magnifier and haptic-touch behavior during a 350ms hold can only be checked on an iPhone.
3. **Scroll-stop taps:** the 100ms guard is a heuristic. A scroll that glides very slowly might not send scroll events often enough to trip it.
4. **Touchscreen laptops:** a finger on the screen gets long-press behavior, while the trackpad doesn't change. Mention this in the PR.
5. **Existing mouse issue, not in scope:** if pointer capture is lost mid-drag and the mouse is released outside the rows, the drag can get stuck. That's true today too. I'd note it rather than fix it here.
6. **Discoverability:** there's no hint that a long press starts a drag, which the issue also doesn't cover.

## How each criterion gets verified

| # | Unit test | Browser or device check |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Swipe scrolls, never selects | Tests 5, 7, 9 | Swipe on a cell (emulation and phones) |
| 2. Hold, then drag, same behavior as #70 | Tests 2–4, 6, 15 | Hold, drag, and auto-scroll on phones |
| 3. No scrolling under the finger during a drag | Test 13 | Phones: the page stays still during a drag |
| 4. No menu, callout or text selection | Test 14 and the grid class test | iPhone (callout) and Android (menu) |
| 5. Mouse unchanged | Test 1 and all existing tests | Laptop trackpad and mouse |
| 6. Automated tests for hold, movement, and mouse vs. touch | Tests 1–15 | — |

**Decision needed:** keep tap-to-toggle with the scroll guard (my recommendation), or make a tap do nothing. Once you pick, I can write the code and tests. I'll leave all commits to you.

```text
/**
 * jsdom does not implement PointerEvent, so `fireEvent.pointerDown` etc. fall back to a plain Event
 * without `pointerId`, `pointerType` or `isPrimary`. This minimal stand-in fills those in for tests.
 */
export function installPointerEventPolyfill(): void {
  if (typeof window.PointerEvent !== "undefined") return;

  class PointerEventPolyfill extends MouseEvent {
    pointerId: number;
    pointerType: string;
    isPrimary: boolean;

    constructor(type: string, init: PointerEventInit = {}) {
      super(type, init);
      this.pointerId = init.pointerId ?? 1;
      this.pointerType = init.pointerType ?? "mouse";
      this.isPrimary = init.isPrimary ?? true;
    }
  }

  Object.defineProperty(window, "PointerEvent", { value: PointerEventPolyfill, configurable: true });
}

/**
 * Scroll speed (px per frame) while dragging near the scroll container's edges:
 * negative near the top, positive near the bottom, faster the closer to the edge.
 */
export function getAutoScrollSpeed(
  pointerY: number,
  top: number,
  bottom: number,
  edgeSize = 40,
  maxSpeed = 16
): number {
  const distanceIntoTopEdge = top + edgeSize - pointerY;
  if (distanceIntoTopEdge > 0) {
    return -Math.max(1, Math.round(maxSpeed * Math.min(1, distanceIntoTopEdge / edgeSize)));
  }
  const distanceIntoBottomEdge = pointerY - (bottom - edgeSize);
  if (distanceIntoBottomEdge > 0) {
    return Math.max(1, Math.round(maxSpeed * Math.min(1, distanceIntoBottomEdge / edgeSize)));
  }
  return 0;
}
```

```text
The warning means Chrome received a `preventDefault()` call on a touchmove event that couldn't be cancelled. Chrome ignores the call because the page is already scrolling. It appears when an attempt to cancel a touchmove event with cancelable=false is ignored, for example because scrolling is in progress and cannot be interrupted.

**Why Chrome does this:** Chrome's scrolling intervention, introduced in Chrome 56, makes touch listeners passive by default so scrolling starts faster. DevTools logs a warning when you call preventDefault() in an event where the intervention is active. The same message can also appear for touchstart and touchend events. One Mapbox contributor noted that it fires for touchmove and touchend and there's reports that it also fires for touchstart.

**Common fixes:**
- **Check `event.cancelable` first.** Only call `preventDefault()` when the flag is true. One guide shows this pattern: if (event.cancelable) { event.preventDefault(); } inside the touch handler.
- **Opt out of passive mode explicitly.** If you truly need to block scrolling, register the listener with `{passive: false}`. Be aware that this blocks the fast-scroll path. Chrome's own guidance is to use CSS `touch-action` to control gestures instead, and to keep calling `preventDefault` only for browsers that don't support `touch-action`.
- **Remove unnecessary calls.** In the Syncfusion forum case, the warning came from a line that cancelled a click-related event, and removing that line resolved the problem.

**Is it harmful?** Often not. Several developers reported it as log noise. One Framework7 user said just ignore it, not the issue really, and a Chinese DCloud forum post said it doesn't affect normal functionality. Mapbox treated it as a fair bit of log spam and fixed it in their code.

**Caveat:** The search didn't return Chromium's source code or the official spec text for this exact message. The explanations above come from developer blogs, forums, and Chrome's 2017 scrolling-intervention post, so check the current Chrome documentation if you need the authoritative behavior for your version.
```

# Issue #93: technical review before implementation

**Recommendation:** go ahead, but in stages. Mouse and trackpad are safe because the branch on pointer type happens before any shared code, and mouse input ignores `touch-action`. The core touch mechanism (pointer events for tracking, plus a non-passive `touchmove` listener to block scrolling) is a common pattern, but no spec guarantees it. I also found a pen risk that the earlier plan missed. Confirm both on real devices before writing the full implementation and tests.

Labels used below: **[code]** confirmed by reading the code, **[docs]** backed by specs or library documentation (sources at the end), **[assumption]** my reasoning without evidence, **[device]** can only be confirmed on hardware.

## 1. Existing implementation

### Event walkthrough (`useWeeklyGridDrag.ts`) [code]

**`pointerdown` (lines 128–147):**
- Returns early if the grid is read-only (no `onSelectionChange`) or the pointer isn't the primary one.
- For mouse, ignores any button except the left one.
- `readCellPosition` uses `closest("[data-day][data-slot]")`, so presses on hour labels do nothing.
- Then it calls `preventDefault()` and `setPointerCapture` on the rows container (using `?.`), records the Y position, and creates the drag state. The mode is `"deselect"` if the pressed cell is already selected, otherwise `"select"`.

**`pointermove` (149–157):** does nothing without a drag. Otherwise it updates the Y position, calls `followPointer`, and calls `autoScroll.startIfNeeded()`.

**`pointerup` (159–176):**
- Does nothing without a drag.
- Calls `endDrag()`, applies the drag to that day's slots, and skips the callback if nothing changed.
- Otherwise it reports `{ day, startMinute, endMinute, mode }`.

**`pointercancel` (198):** calls `endDrag`, so the preview disappears and nothing is saved.

**Missing check:** neither `pointermove` nor `pointerup` checks `pointerId`. Only `pointerdown` checks `isPrimary`.

### How selection, preview and auto-scroll work [code]

- **Same column:** `followPointer` (110–119) only uses vertical position. It turns Y into a slot using the rows' bounding box and clamps it to 0–95, so the drag stays in the starting day's column.
- **Select and deselect:** `applyDragToSlots` in `lib/weekly-grid.ts` (lines 99–112) sets every slot between the start slot and the current slot to the mode's value.
- **Preview:** `preview` (178–184) and `getDisplaySlots` (186–189) show the change before it's saved. The grid colors cells from these values.
- **Auto-scroll:** `useEdgeAutoScroll` (42–82) runs an animation-frame loop. `getAutoScrollSpeed` (`weekly-grid.ts` line 189) uses a 40px edge zone and a maximum of 16px per frame. It sets `scrollTop` directly and calls `followPointer` after each step.
- **Wiring in the grid:** handlers are only attached when the grid is editable (`WeeklyAvailabilityGrid.tsx` line 93). The container gets `select-none` when editable, and cells get `cursor-pointer touch-none` (line 125).

### What stays the same and what changes

**Unchanged** [code]:
- In the hook: `readCellPosition`, `hasSelectionChanged`, `useEdgeAutoScroll`, `followPointer`, `endDrag`, `preview` and `getDisplaySlots`.
- All of `lib/weekly-grid.ts`.
- `AvailabilitySettings.tsx`.

**Changes:**
- `onPointerDown` (128–147): its body moves into a shared `startDrag()`, and it gains a touch branch.
- `onPointerMove` (149–157): hold-tolerance check and a `pointerId` check.
- `onPointerUp` (159–176): the commit logic moves into `commitDrag()`, and it handles an unfinished hold.
- `onPointerCancel` (198): also cancels a pending hold.
- One new `useEffect` for the native listeners and cleanup.
- The returned `handlers` (194–199) gain `onContextMenu`.
- Grid lines 124–125: the comment and class change.

## 2. Mouse, trackpad and pen

**Mouse clicks still toggle one cell.** Mouse goes straight to `startDrag()`, which is today's code moved without changes, and `commitDrag()` is today's commit code. The existing test "toggles a single slot on click" (hook test line 168) covers this. [code]

**Mouse and trackpad drags still start immediately.** Trackpads report `pointerType: "mouse"`, and two-finger trackpad scrolling uses wheel events, which this change doesn't touch. [assumption, standard browser behavior]

**Touchscreen laptops support both.** Each pointer is handled by its own type, so the trackpad starts drags immediately and a finger on the screen uses the long press. [code] Whether the finger part works depends on the browser (section 4). [device]

**Pen may not behave exactly as before. This is a risk I hadn't raised earlier.** Its JavaScript path is unchanged, since it goes straight to `startDrag()`. [code] The difference is the CSS:
- Today, `touch-none` stops the browser from scrolling during a pen drag.
- Browsers can treat a pen like a finger for scrolling. The spec calls both "direct manipulation" pointers, and Apple Pencil scrolls pages in Safari. [docs + assumption]
- With `touch-pan-y`, a vertical pen drag could be taken over as a scroll. The browser would fire `pointercancel` and the pen drag would be discarded.
- The `touchmove` blocker runs whenever a drag is active, whatever the input type. It would protect pen drags only if the browser also sends touch events for the pen. I believe Safari does for Apple Pencil, but I haven't verified this, and I'm less sure about Windows pens. [assumption, device]
- If pen drags break, the options are: give pen the long-press too (changes pen behavior), or accept the regression for the browsers affected.

**Could a shared change affect desktop?**
- `touch-action` doesn't affect mouse input. [docs]
- The `touchmove` listener never sees mouse events.
- `onContextMenu → preventDefault` is shared, so **right-click on an editable cell would no longer show the browser menu.** Right-click doesn't start a drag today either (line 131), so only the menu disappears. The handler could limit it to touch, but `contextmenu` events don't reliably report the pointer type, so the simpler choice is to block it on editable cells. [code + assumption] Please confirm this is acceptable.

## 3. Touch behavior

**Hold timer and movement threshold:**
1. On a touch `pointerdown`: store `{ pointerId, position, mode, startX, startY }` and start a 350ms `setTimeout`. Don't call `preventDefault` and don't capture the pointer.
2. On `pointermove` for that pointer during the hold: update the Y position. If the finger has moved more than 8px from the start (`Math.hypot`), cancel the hold.
3. When the timer fires: run the same `startDrag(position, y, rows, pointerId)` the mouse uses, with pointer capture in a try/catch.

**Quick taps keep toggling without breaking scrolling:**
- If `pointerup` arrives during the hold, the finger moved 8px or less, and no `pointercancel` came, call `commitDrag` with the start and end slot equal. This is exactly the same result as a mouse click.
- Swipes never reach this point. They either go over 8px or the browser cancels the pointer to scroll.
- **Guard for taps that stop a scroll:** browsers still fire `pointerdown` and `pointerup` for those taps. To ignore them, a passive capture-phase `scroll` listener on `document` records the time of the last scroll. A tap only toggles if no scroll happened in the ~100ms before it. [assumption: that browsers fire pointer events for these taps, and that 100ms is the right window, both need device testing]

**Multiple fingers, cancellation, early release:**
- A second finger during a hold cancels the hold. This check runs before the existing `!isPrimary` return.
- During a drag, `pointerId` is added to the drag state, and move, up and cancel events from any other pointer are ignored. This also fixes the existing missing check.
- `pointercancel` during a hold clears the timer. During a drag, it behaves as today: discard without saving.
- An early release follows the tap rule above.
- On unmount, the effect cleanup clears the timer and both listeners.
- The timer callback checks a ref for the current `onSelectionChange`, so a grid that has become read-only during a hold doesn't start a drag.

**The original drag logic stays the same.** Both touch and mouse end in the same `startDrag`, `followPointer`, `useEdgeAutoScroll` and `commitDrag`. The drag only ever starts on the pressed cell. [code]

## 4. Browser compatibility

### What the specs and documentation say [docs]

- **No mid-gesture changes:** `touch-action` is fixed when a gesture starts, and changing it afterward has no effect on that gesture (MDN). So the code can't switch cells to `touch-none` once the hold finishes.
- **Pointer events can't stop scrolling:** the Pointer Events spec says scrolling "cannot be suppressed by canceling a pointer event". Pages must declare it with `touch-action` instead.
- **When `pointercancel` fires:** the browser **must** fire it when it decides to use the pointer to pan or zoom the page. Other cases the spec lists include the device or OS interrupting the input, such as an orientation change or a system gesture.
- **The key gap:** the spec says it "does not provide any advice on the expected behavior of user agents that support both Touch Events" and pointer events. The hybrid approach rests on exactly that interaction.
- **Touch events can stop scrolling:** dnd-kit's documentation says "it is possible to prevent the page from scrolling in `touchmove` events," unlike pointer events. react-beautiful-dnd's touch sensor works the same way: scrolling is allowed during the hold, and "a drag has started and we prevent native scrolling." Both libraries listen with **touch events** throughout, not pointer events.
- **Chrome stops honoring cancellation once scrolling has started:** after that, `touchmove` events can't be cancelled, and Chrome logs "Ignored attempt to cancel a touchmove event with cancelable=false". Chrome treats listeners on `window`, `document` and `body` as passive by default, but an element listener with explicit `{ passive: false }` can still cancel.

### What's assumed but not proven

- **[assumption] Blocking the first `touchmove` stops the scroll before it starts.** If the finger hasn't moved more than ~8px before 350ms, the browser shouldn't have started scrolling yet, so the next `touchmove` should still be cancellable. Cancelling it should stop the scroll, so no `pointercancel` would follow and pointer events would keep arriving. This is the behavior people rely on, but no spec promises it for pointer events and touch events together.
- **[assumption] Chrome's scroll threshold is larger than 8px.** If the browser starts scrolling before our tolerance is reached, it fires `pointercancel`, which also cancels the hold. Either way the outcome is safe.

### Per-platform limitations

| Platform | Known limitations | Verified? |
|---|---|---|
| **iOS Safari** | Supports `touch-action` (MDN marks it "Baseline… since September 2019", without per-version detail). The press-and-hold callout needs `-webkit-touch-callout: none`. Text selection is already blocked by `select-none`. | [device] |
| **Android Chrome** | Chrome's own long press, at about 400–500ms, fires `contextmenu` after our 350ms drag has started. Blocking it should keep the touch going, but I have no evidence that Chrome won't also fire `pointercancel`. If it does, every long-press drag is discarded. **This is the biggest risk.** | [device] |
| **Windows touchscreen** | The OS's press-and-hold acts as a right-click (`contextmenu`), which gets blocked. Whether Chrome and Edge fire touch events there, and **whether Firefox on desktop fires them at all**, is unconfirmed. If a browser doesn't fire them, the blocker never runs, a vertical drag after the hold becomes a scroll, and the drag is cancelled. Nothing changes by accident, but the long-press drag wouldn't work there. | [assumption / device] |

### Alternatives compared

| Approach | Reliability | Size | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Pointer events + non-passive `touchmove`** (current plan) | Probably works, but nothing guarantees it | Smallest, one handler path | Needs device confirmation first |
| **B. Touch events for touch, pointer events for mouse and pen** | Documented approach (dnd-kit, react-beautiful-dnd) | About 60–100 more lines: separate touch start, move and end handlers, and pointer handlers must ignore touch | Same drag core, but move and release logic is duplicated |
| **C. "Edit" mode toggle** (`touch-none` only while editing) | Most reliable, no timing tricks | Small, but needs UI and translations | The issue rejected it, since it adds a tap and extra UI state |

**Recommendation:** try A first, as a throwaway change that isn't committed, and test it on an iPhone and an Android phone. If Android's long press cancels the pointer, or the page still scrolls, switch the touch path to B. The drag core and tests barely change either way.

## 5. Implementation scope

Pseudocode diff for the hook:

```ts
const LONG_PRESS_MS = 350;
const LONG_PRESS_MOVE_TOLERANCE_PX = 8;
const TAP_AFTER_SCROLL_GUARD_MS = 100;

type DragState = { pointerId: number; day; anchorSlot; currentSlot; mode };   // + pointerId
type PendingHold = { pointerId; position; mode; x; y; timer };

const pendingHoldRef = useRef<PendingHold | null>(null);
const lastScrollAtRef = useRef(0);
const onSelectionChangeRef = useRef(onSelectionChange); onSelectionChangeRef.current = onSelectionChange;

const startDrag = (position, mode, clientY, element, pointerId) => {   // body of today's lines 137–144
  try { element.setPointerCapture?.(pointerId); } catch { /* touch is implicitly captured; mouse keeps working over rows */ }
  pointerYRef.current = clientY;
  updateDrag({ pointerId, day: position.day, anchorSlot: position.slot, currentSlot: position.slot, mode });
};
const commitDrag = (state) => { /* today's lines 164–175, unchanged */ };
const cancelHold = () => { clearTimeout(pendingHoldRef.current?.timer); pendingHoldRef.current = null; };

onPointerDown(e):
  if (!onSelectionChange) return;
  if (!e.isPrimary) { cancelHold(); return; }                     // second finger cancels a hold
  if (e.pointerType === "mouse" && e.button !== 0) return;
  position = readCellPosition(e.target); if (!position) return;
  mode = value[day]?.[slot] ? "deselect" : "select";
  if (e.pointerType !== "touch") { e.preventDefault(); startDrag(...); return; }   // mouse and pen: today's path
  const { clientX, clientY, pointerId, currentTarget, timeStamp } = e;
  pendingHoldRef.current = { pointerId, position, mode, x: clientX, y: clientY, downAt: timeStamp,
    timer: setTimeout(() => { pendingHoldRef.current = null;
      if (onSelectionChangeRef.current) startDrag(position, mode, pointerYRef.current, currentTarget, pointerId); }, LONG_PRESS_MS) };
  pointerYRef.current = clientY;

onPointerMove(e):
  hold = pendingHoldRef.current;
  if (hold?.pointerId === e.pointerId) { pointerYRef.current = e.clientY;
    if (Math.hypot(e.clientX - hold.x, e.clientY - hold.y) > TOLERANCE) cancelHold(); return; }
  if (dragRef.current?.pointerId !== e.pointerId) return;
  ...today's lines 152–154

onPointerUp(e):
  hold = pendingHoldRef.current;
  if (hold?.pointerId === e.pointerId) { cancelHold();
    if (hold.downAt - lastScrollAtRef.current > GUARD) commitDrag({ ...hold.position as anchor=current, mode: hold.mode }); return; }
  if (dragRef.current?.pointerId !== e.pointerId) return;
  ...today's code via commitDrag

onPointerCancel(e): cancelHold(); if (dragRef.current?.pointerId === e.pointerId) endDrag();

useEffect(() => {
  const rows = rowsRef.current;
  const blockScroll = (e: TouchEvent) => { if (dragRef.current && e.cancelable) e.preventDefault(); };
  const noteScroll = () => { lastScrollAtRef.current = performance.now(); };
  rows?.addEventListener("touchmove", blockScroll, { passive: false });
  document.addEventListener("scroll", noteScroll, { capture: true, passive: true });
  return () => { cancelHold(); rows?.removeEventListener(...); document.removeEventListener(...); };
}, [rowsRef]);

handlers: { ..., onContextMenu: (e) => e.preventDefault() }
```

Two details in that sketch:
- `e.timeStamp` and `performance.now()` both count from page load, so the scroll guard can compare them. [docs: DOM `timeStamp` is a high-resolution time]
- The `e.cancelable` check prevents Chrome's warning in the rare case where a drag starts after a scroll is already under way.

Grid component:

```diff
- // Lets a finger drag select instead of scrolling; labels and header still scroll
- isEditable && "cursor-pointer touch-none"
+ // Swipes scroll; a long press starts a drag (see useWeeklyGridDrag). The callout would cover the grid on iOS
+ isEditable && "cursor-pointer touch-pan-y [-webkit-touch-callout:none]"
```

**Nothing new in React state.** The plan adds 3 refs, 1 effect and 3 constants, and moves two pieces of code into functions. If the team decides a tap should do nothing, the scroll listener, its ref and the tap branch can all go.

**Drag and auto-scroll code:** neither changes. Only the code that starts and ends a drag changes. [code]

**Accessibility and keyboard:**
- The grid has no keyboard interaction today. Cells aren't focusable and there's no `onKeyDown`, so nothing changes here. [code]
- Cell `aria-label`s and `aria-readonly` are unchanged. [code]
- Whether VoiceOver or TalkBack can activate cells, before or after this change, is unverified. [device]
- Long-press drag has no visible hint. That's outside the issue's scope.

In jsdom, touch input is simulated by passing `pointerType: "touch"` through the existing test polyfill. [code]

**Chrome DevTools touch emulation (manual):**
- A swipe on a cell scrolls the grid and the page without selecting anything.
- Hold, drag and auto-scroll all work.
- A move before 350ms cancels the hold.
- A tap toggles one cell.
- The page doesn't move during a drag.
- With emulation off, mouse and trackpad behave as before.
- Emulation doesn't reproduce Android's long-press menu, iOS's callout, or real momentum scrolling.

**Physical devices:**
- **iPhone, Safari:** callout, text-selection magnifier, scroll versus drag, and taps that stop a scroll.
- **Android, Chrome:** the long-press `contextmenu` and `pointercancel` question (the biggest risk), and taps that stop a scroll.
- **Touchscreen laptop (Chrome, Edge, Firefox):** finger long-press, while the trackpad stays unchanged.
- **iPad with Apple Pencil, or a Windows pen:** the pen regression question.
- On a phone, open the local dev server over the same Wi-Fi.

**Showing the grid without committing #71 work:**
- The settings page is rendered from `apps/web/modules/availability/[schedule]/schedule-view.tsx`.
- Locally, either pass `availabilityView="grid"` there, or change the default at `AvailabilitySettings.tsx` line 352.
- Don't stage that file. Revert it with `git restore <file>` before committing. Adding just your four files with `git add` keeps it out.

## 7. Final assessment

| Criterion | Implementation | Verification | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. A swipe scrolls and never selects | `touch-pan-y`, the 8px cancel, cancel on `pointercancel`, the scroll guard | Unit tests, DevTools, phones | Logic [code]; real scrolling [device] |
| 2. Hold ~350ms, then drag, same as #70 | Timer calls the shared `startDrag`; drag and auto-scroll code unchanged | Unit tests, DevTools, phones | Logic [code]; drag continuing after the hold [device] |
| 3. No scrolling under the finger during a drag | Non-passive `touchmove` on rows | Unit test (`defaultPrevented`), phones | Approach [docs]; mixed with pointer events [assumption → device] |
| 4. No menu, callout or selection | `onContextMenu`, `-webkit-touch-callout`, existing `select-none` | Unit and grid tests, iPhone and Android | [device] |
| 5. Mouse unchanged | Branch before shared code, mouse ignores `touch-action` | Existing tests unchanged, laptop check | [code + docs]. Pen is a separate risk |
| 6. Automated tests | The tests listed above | `TZ=UTC yarn vitest run packages/features/schedules` | Not written yet |

### Open risks and decisions

1. **Android Chrome long press** may cancel the pointer: needs a device test. If it does, use approach B.
2. **Mixing pointer and touch events** isn't specified anywhere: needs a device test, with B as the fallback.
3. **Pen regression** under `touch-pan-y`: needs a pen device. If it fails, decide whether pen also uses the long press.
4. **Right-click menu** is removed on editable cells: decide whether that's acceptable.
5. **Tap behavior:** keep tap-to-toggle with the scroll guard (my recommendation), or make a tap do nothing.
6. **Windows touchscreens and desktop Firefox** may not fire touch events: test if possible. If not, at least the result is safe.
7. **Existing issue, out of scope:** if the mouse loses pointer capture and is released outside the rows, the drag can get stuck.

### Is it safe to proceed?

Yes, in this order:
1. Make the throwaway version of A, uncommitted, and check the three device questions: Android long press, iOS scroll blocking, and pen.
2. If they pass, write the code and tests as described.
3. If not, switch the touch path to B. The tests stay the same, since they check behavior rather than which events are used.

Mouse and trackpad are low risk because of the early branch and because mouse ignores `touch-action`. The touch and pen parts are where the real uncertainty is, and they fail safe: a cancelled drag never saves anything.

**Confirmed from code:** everything in sections 1 and 5 marked [code], the test lines that need updating, the missing `pointerId` check today, and where the grid is rendered.
**Assumptions:** the scroll-threshold ordering, browsers firing pointer events for scroll-stopping taps, pen producing touch events, and Windows touch-event support.
**Only verifiable on devices:** criteria 1, 3 and 4 in real browsers, the Android long press, the iOS callout, and pen behavior.

I haven't edited, committed or pushed anything.

Sources:
- [W3C Pointer Events Level 3](https://www.w3.org/TR/pointerevents3/)
- [MDN: touch-action](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/touch-action)

- [react-beautiful-dnd touch sensor docs](https://github.com/atlassian/react-beautiful-dnd/blob/master/docs/sensors/touch.md)
- [Chrome: Making touch scrolling fast by default](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/scrolling-intervention)
- [Uriports: "Ignored attempt to cancel a touchmove event with cancelable=false"](https://uriports.com/blog/easy-fix-for-intervention-ignored-attempt-to-cancel-a-touchmove-event-with-cancelable-false)

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-29 02:07:11Z)**_

I built the Option A proof of concept in three files (+148 / −37) and haven't committed or pushed anything. The 239 existing tests in `packages/features/schedules` still pass. I didn't add the document scroll listener or the 100ms scroll guard. Whether the long press really hands over to a drag can only be confirmed in a browser, so the DevTools steps below are the real test.

## What changed

**`hooks/useWeeklyGridDrag.ts`**
- **Mouse and pen:** they still start dragging on press. The press code is the same as before; it just records the `pointerId` and hands off to a small `startDrag()` helper.
- **Touch press:** starts a 350ms timer instead of a drag. It doesn't block the browser or capture the pointer, so the browser can still scroll.
- **When the timer fires:** it captures the pointer (a failure there is caught and ignored) and starts the same drag a mouse would.
- **Movement during the hold:** more than 8px from the start point cancels it.
- **Quick tap:** lifting before 350ms toggles one slot, exactly like a mouse click today.
- **Matching pointer:** move, up and cancel events only affect the pointer that started the hold or drag. A second finger during a hold cancels the hold. A second finger's events during a drag are ignored.
- **`pointercancel`:** only acts when its `pointerId` matches, as you asked.
- **Scroll blocking:** a native `touchmove` listener on the rows calls `preventDefault()`, but only during a drag and only if the event can still be cancelled. Its cleanup also clears the hold timer on unmount.
- **Context menu:** the browser menu is blocked only for touch, or while a hold or drag is in progress. Right-clicking on desktop still shows the menu.
- **Unchanged:** selection, deselection, preview and auto-scroll logic.

**`components/WeeklyAvailabilityGrid.tsx`:** the cell class changed from `touch-none` to `touch-pan-y [-webkit-touch-callout:none]`, and I updated its comment.

**`components/WeeklyAvailabilityGrid.test.tsx`:** I updated the two class assertions and the test name for the new CSS. No other test changed.

## Checks

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `TZ=UTC yarn vitest run packages/features/schedules` | **8 files, 239 passed, 4 skipped** (the skips were already there) |
| Hook and grid tests again, after the last edit | **23/23 passed** |
| `tsc` on `packages/features` | **No errors in the changed files.** The package already has errors in unrelated files, such as `business-days-plugin.ts` and `TimezoneSelectComponent.tsx`. |
| Biome lint | 1 warning: the hook is now 145 lines (limit 100). I'd split the touch logic into its own small hook in the full implementation. |
| Biome format | Reports every line in all three files. That's Windows line endings: you have `core.autocrlf=true`, and the diff itself has no CR characters, so it's not from this change. |

All existing tests still use the mouse, so they confirm desktop behavior didn't change. **The touch path has no unit tests yet.** I left those for the full implementation, as planned.

## Pen and `touch-pan-y`

- **Pen's code is unchanged:** it never goes through the timer and still calls `preventDefault()` and captures the pointer on press.
- **The CSS change could still affect pen.** `touch-pan-y` lets the browser scroll vertically for any pointer it treats like a finger. Previously `touch-none` blocked that for everything. If a browser handles a vertical pen stroke as a scroll, it fires `pointercancel` and the pen drag is discarded without saving.
- **What could still protect pen:** the `touchmove` blocker runs during any drag, so it would protect pen drags if the browser also sends touch events for the pen. I believe Safari does this for Apple Pencil, but I haven't verified it. For Windows pens I don't know.
- **DevTools can't emulate a pen**, so this needs an iPad with Apple Pencil or a Windows pen device.
- **If pen does break,** either give pen the long press too (changes pen behavior), or put `touch-none` back on cells while a drag is active. The second doesn't help, because the browser decides `touch-action` when the gesture starts. So realistically it's the first option or accepting the regression.

## Testing with Chrome DevTools touch emulation

**1. Show the grid (temporary, don't commit).** In `apps/web/modules/availability/[schedule]/schedule-view.tsx`, add a prop to the `<AvailabilitySettings` call at line 109:
```tsx
<AvailabilitySettings
  availabilityView="grid"
  schedule={schedule}
```
Undo it afterwards with `git restore "apps/web/modules/availability/[schedule]/schedule-view.tsx"`.

**2. Open the grid.** Run `yarn dev`, log in (for example `pro` / `pro`), go to **Availability**, and open a schedule.

**3. Turn on touch emulation.** In DevTools, press Ctrl+Shift+M and choose **Pixel 7** (or iPhone 14), then **reload**. Check that `matchMedia("(pointer: coarse)").matches` returns `true` in the console.

**4. Add event logging.** Paste this in the console:
```js
const rows = document.querySelector('[role="rowgroup"]');
monitorEvents(rows, ["pointerdown", "pointerup", "pointercancel", "contextmenu"]);
rows.addEventListener("touchmove", (e) => console.log("touchmove cancelable:", e.cancelable, "prevented:", e.defaultPrevented));
```
The logging listener is added after the hook's, so `prevented` shows whether the hook blocked the scroll.

**5. Run these checks:**

| # | Action | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| A | Quick swipe up or down starting on a cell | The grid or page scrolls, and no cell changes. The log shows `pointercancel` and `prevented: false`. |
| B | Press a cell, hold still about half a second, then drag down | The pressed cell highlights when the hold completes, and cells fill as you drag. **No `pointercancel`**, `touchmove` shows `prevented: true`, the page doesn't move, and the change saves on release. **This is the main thing the proof of concept tests.** |
| C | Like B, but on an already-selected cell | Cells are deselected. |
| D | Like B, and drag to the bottom edge of the grid | The grid auto-scrolls and the selection keeps extending. |
| E | Like B, but drag sideways into another day | The selection stays in the starting day. |
| F | Press, then move about 10px sideways before the hold completes | No drag starts, and nothing changes on release. |
| G | Quick tap on a cell | That one slot toggles. |
| H | Hold about 1s without moving | `contextmenu` may be logged, but no menu appears. |
| I | Turn off the Device Toolbar (Ctrl+Shift+M) and reload, then click, drag and right-click with the mouse | Clicks toggle, drags start immediately, and **right-click still shows the browser menu**. |

## What DevTools can't show

- **Android Chrome:** whether its own long-press handling (around 400–500ms) fires `pointercancel` during a drag. This is still the biggest risk, and if it happens, Option B is the fallback.
- **iOS Safari:** the callout, the text-selection magnifier, and real momentum scrolling.
- **Pen:** iPad with Apple Pencil, or a Windows pen.
- **Taps that stop a scroll:** with no scroll guard, tapping to stop a gliding scroll can toggle a cell. This is expected for now.

## Gaps left for the full implementation

- No unit tests for the touch path yet.
- If the grid becomes read-only during a hold, the timer can still start a drag.
- The scroll guard isn't added.
- Splitting the touch logic out of the hook would clear the Biome function-length warning.

If B passes with no `pointercancel` in DevTools and on a real phone, Option A holds up and I can write the full implementation with tests next.

The proof of concept adds 140 lines and removes 31. About **87 of the added lines are new behavior**. The other **~53 are code I moved or reorganized**. A simpler version can keep every safety check at roughly **+70 / −8**, about half the current change. Mouse, trackpad, pen, selection and auto-scroll behave exactly as they do now in both versions.

## Where the 140 added lines come from

**New behavior, about 87 lines:**

| Piece | Lines | Needed? |
|---|---|---|
| Constants, plus `ReactMouseEvent` import | 5 | Yes |
| `pointerId` on `DragState` | 1 | Yes, for the matching-pointer checks |
| `PendingTouchHold` type | 6 | Yes, though it can be smaller |
| Hold ref and `cancelTouchHold` | 9 | Yes |
| Second finger cancels the hold | 5 | Yes |
| Touch branch in `onPointerDown` | 19 | Yes, but 7 of those lines can go (see below) |
| Hold branch and pointer check in `onPointerMove` | 8 | Yes |
| Tap branch and pointer check in `onPointerUp` | 8 | Yes |
| `onPointerCancel` with matching `pointerId` | 9 | Yes |
| `onContextMenu` | 6 | Yes |
| Native `touchmove` listener and unmount cleanup | 12 | Yes |
| New `handlers` entries | 2 | Yes |

**Moved or reorganized, about 53 lines:**

| Piece | Lines | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| `commitDrag` | 18 | The 13-line commit body moved out of `onPointerUp`, plus a `useCallback` wrapper, so a tap could reuse it |
| `startDrag` | 9 | A wrapper around 2 existing lines |
| `DragStart` type | 2 | Only exists to support `startDrag` and `commitDrag` |
| `onPointerDown` | ~12 | The press code was reorganized into a `start` object and a mouse branch. The 3 lines that block text selection and capture the pointer were moved unchanged. |
| `onPointerUp` | ~6 | Reformatted to accept the event |
| Dependency arrays, blank lines | ~6 | Follow-on changes |

Of the 31 removed lines, about 25 reappear elsewhere: 13 in `commitDrag`, plus the moved `onPointerDown` lines. Only about 6 lines of old code were actually replaced.

## What's redundant

1. **`commitDrag` isn't needed.** A quick tap is just a drag that never moved. On `pointerup`, if a hold is pending, cancel it and use the pending drag as the drag to finish. The existing release code then runs unchanged.
   - This keeps the original 13 lines in place and reduces the `onPointerUp` change to about 5 lines.
   - When there's no active drag, `endDrag()` sets state that's already `null`, which React skips.
2. **`startDrag` and `DragStart` aren't needed.** Build the full `DragState` once at the top of `onPointerDown`. Mouse and pen call `updateDrag(drag)` right where they always have. The timer calls `updateDrag(drag)` too. The pending hold stores `{ drag, startX, startY, timer }`, so neither the extra type nor the `{ ...hold, currentSlot }` spread is needed.
3. **Explicit pointer capture for touch, the try/catch around it, and the `rows` variable aren't needed (6 lines).** The Pointer Events spec says touch input is captured automatically to the element it pressed, so every move, up and cancel still reaches the rows container.
   - Mouse keeps its explicit capture exactly as it is now.
   - This depends on browsers following that part of the spec, which DevTools check E covers (drag outside the grid; the selection should keep following).
4. **Updating `pointerYRef` during the hold isn't needed (2 lines).** Everything that reads it (`followPointer` and auto-scroll) only runs after a `pointermove` has already set it.

## What has to stay

- **`pointerId` checks** in move, up and cancel. Without them a second finger can take over or end a drag, and you asked for them on cancel.
- **The second finger cancelling the hold.** `pan-y` doesn't allow pinch-zoom, so two still fingers would otherwise start a drag after 350ms.
- **`cancelTouchHold()` at the start of a touch press.** It's one line, and it's the only protection against a timer being left running if events were somehow lost.
- **The 8px tolerance check.** Sideways movement is the case the browser doesn't cancel for us under `pan-y`.
- **`onContextMenu`'s touch check.** On a Windows touchscreen, the press-and-hold menu may only appear after you lift your finger. By then no hold or drag is active, so this check is the only thing that blocks it, and only in browsers that report the pointer type on `contextmenu`. Removing it saves 1 line and risks a menu after every long-press drag.
- **The `touchmove` listener and its `cancelable` check.** These are what block scrolling. The check also avoids Chrome's warning in the console.
- **Clearing the timer on unmount.**

## Smaller version

```ts
// Touch drags wait for a long press so a finger swiping across the grid scrolls instead of selecting
const LONG_PRESS_MS = 350;
const LONG_PRESS_MOVE_TOLERANCE_PX = 8;

type DragState = { pointerId: number; day: number; anchorSlot: number; currentSlot: number; mode: SlotDragMode };
type PendingTouchHold = { drag: DragState; startX: number; startY: number; timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> };

const pendingTouchHoldRef = useRef<PendingTouchHold | null>(null);
const cancelTouchHold = useCallback(() => {
  if (pendingTouchHoldRef.current) clearTimeout(pendingTouchHoldRef.current.timer);
  pendingTouchHoldRef.current = null;
}, []);

onPointerDown:
  if (!onSelectionChange) return;
  if (!event.isPrimary) {
    // A second finger means a pinch or multi-touch gesture, not a long press
    cancelTouchHold();
    return;
  }
  if (event.pointerType === "mouse" && event.button !== 0) return;      // unchanged
  const position = readCellPosition(event.target);                      // unchanged
  if (!position) return;                                                // unchanged
  const drag: DragState = { pointerId: event.pointerId, day, anchorSlot, currentSlot, mode }; // the existing literal, moved up
  if (event.pointerType === "touch") {

    cancelTouchHold();
    const timer = setTimeout(() => { pendingTouchHoldRef.current = null; updateDrag(drag); }, LONG_PRESS_MS);
    pendingTouchHoldRef.current = { drag, startX: event.clientX, startY: event.clientY, timer };
    return;
  }
  // Stops text selection and native drag-and-drop from starting           // unchanged
  event.preventDefault();                                               // unchanged
  event.currentTarget.setPointerCapture?.(event.pointerId);             // unchanged
  pointerYRef.current = event.clientY;                                  // unchanged
  updateDrag(drag);

onPointerMove:
  const hold = pendingTouchHoldRef.current;
  if (hold?.drag.pointerId === event.pointerId) {
    if (Math.hypot(event.clientX - hold.startX, event.clientY - hold.startY) > LONG_PRESS_MOVE_TOLERANCE_PX) cancelTouchHold();
    return;
  }
  if (dragRef.current?.pointerId !== event.pointerId) return;
  ...unchanged

onPointerUp(event):
  let current = dragRef.current;
  const hold = pendingTouchHoldRef.current;
  if (hold?.drag.pointerId === event.pointerId) {
    // A quick tap is a drag that never moved, so it toggles one slot like a mouse click
    cancelTouchHold();
    current = hold.drag;
  }

onPointerCancel, onContextMenu, useEffect: same as the proof of concept
```

## Comparison

| | Current proof of concept | Smaller version |
|---|---|---|
| Diff in the hook | +140 / −31 | about +70 / −8 |
| Mouse and pen code | Reorganized into `startDrag`. Same behavior, but a reviewer has to check that. | The original lines stay where they are, apart from the moved drag object |
| Release code | Moved into `commitDrag` | Unchanged |
| Touch pointer capture | Explicit, with try/catch | Relies on the browser's automatic touch capture (in the spec; DevTools check E confirms it) |
| New names to learn | `startDrag`, `commitDrag`, `DragStart`, `PendingTouchHold`, `cancelTouchHold` | `PendingTouchHold`, `cancelTouchHold` |
| Safety checks | All | All the same ones |
| Biome function-length warning | Yes (145 lines, limit 100) | Probably still over 100. Clearing it would mean splitting the touch logic into a separate hook, which needs access to `dragRef` and `updateDrag`. I'd accept the warning rather than add that. |

**Tradeoffs of the smaller version:**
- **Explicit capture:** it gives up a second line of defense that the spec says isn't needed. If check E fails in some browser, add those 6 lines back.
- **Tap handling:** treating a tap as a drag that never moved is a little less obvious than a named `commitDrag`, so it needs the one-line comment.

I'd go with the smaller version. It keeps every safety check and leaves mouse and pen code almost untouched, which makes "desktop behavior is unchanged" easy for a reviewer to confirm. The release logic also stays the same code that #70's tests already cover. I haven't modified any files. Say the word and I'll rewrite the proof of concept this way and rerun the tests.

```text
I couldn't find a single Firefox bug that covers all of this together, but several related threads are relevant.

**Spec background:** MDN says that for touchscreen browsers that allow direct manipulation, an implicit pointer capture will be called on the element when a pointerdown event triggers. A W3C discussion also notes that browsers MAY implement their own implicit pointer capture behaviour, for example for touch taps on native form controls.

**Firefox-specific bugs:**
- **Bug 1885232 (duplicate-target bug):** Bug 1903889, filed against Firefox 127, is titled "setPointerCapture causes clicks on other elements on pointerup" and was resolved as a duplicate of bug 1885232. A blog note also says that in Firefox, some events of the target element's descendant elements will be incorrectly triggered, citing that bug. This is probably the most relevant thread for your query, but I could not read bug 1885232 itself, so check its current status directly.
- **Bug 1912812:** This reports that Firefox uses 0 for mouse, but Chrome and Safari use 1 for mouse, which makes a setPointerCapture call work only on Firefox in that example. It is a pointerId inconsistency, not a touch-specific issue.
- **Implicit capture tests:** Firefox's test suite has a file that enables a `dom.w3c_pointer_events.implicit_capture` preference for cross-origin iframe touch tests. Searchfox's metadata also marks several same-origin frame touch capture tests as expected: FAIL.
- **Direct manipulation groundwork:** In an older bug, a Mozilla commenter noted that to support gesture with touch event, we have to support Direct Manipulation API (bug 890878). Bug 979345, which implements `manipulation` in Gecko, was also filed from the W3C discussion, though I didn't verify its current status.

**Cross-browser issue:** A W3C mailing list post reports a touch-specific problem where pointer is captured implicitly (touch), and a child element releasing capture doesn't let the parent take over. The poster tested on iOS Safari, Firefox, Chrome, and Edge. A reply explains that when the event bubbles and parent calls setpointercapture it effectively steals the capture, so the child stops receiving events.

For current status, I'd check bug 1885232 and the Firefox Nightly test results on Searchfox, since I didn't see recent updates on the implicit-capture-with-touch cases.
```

<summary>Tool use: **WebFetch**</summary>
 `https://www.w3.org/TR/pointerevents3/`

```text
**Implicit pointer capture (§ 9.4)**

Direct-manipulation inputs such as touch or stylus should act as if pointer capture were set on the target just before `pointerdown` listeners run: "SHOULD behave exactly as if setPointerCapture was called on the target element" and "just before the invocation of any pointerdown listeners." Scripts can check this with `hasPointerCapture`. If capture is not released before the next pointer event fires, a `gotpointercapture` event goes to the target.

**Implicit release (§ 9.5)**

- **After pointerup or pointercancel:** The user agent "MUST clear the pending pointer capture target override for the pointerId" of that event, then processes pending capture, which may fire `lostpointercapture`.
- **Removed element:** "When the pointer capture target override is no longer connected," it "SHOULD be set to the document." A similar rule applies to the pending override, which "SHOULD be cleared" when disconnected. The result is a `lostpointercapture` event fired at the document after the capture node is removed.
- **Pointer lock:** When pointer lock is successfully applied, the user agent "MUST run the steps as if the releasePointerCapture method has been called."

The spec does not list element removal as an explicit release trigger in § 9.5. It instead describes retargeting the capture to the document.

**MAY/SHOULD vs. MUST**

- **Required (MUST):** Clearing the pending override after pointerup/pointercancel, and treating pointer lock as a release.
- **Recommended (SHOULD):** The implicit capture behavior itself in § 9.4, and retargeting or clearing overrides when the element is disconnected in § 9.5.
- **Optional (MAY):** A note in § 9.4 says user agents "may implement implicit pointer capture behavior for all input devices on specific UI widgets," such as range inputs. This is the only place the content uses MAY for capture.
```

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-29 02:24:17Z)**_

I've switched the proof of concept to the smaller version but kept explicit touch pointer capture, because it does add reliability for this grid. The 239 existing schedules tests pass, there are no new TypeScript errors, and Biome adds one function-length warning and two informational notes. Nothing is committed or pushed.

## Implicit vs. explicit pointer capture: kept explicit

After the long press, the hook still calls `setPointerCapture` on the rows container, inside a try/catch.

- **The spec only recommends it.** The Pointer Events spec says browsers *SHOULD* capture touch to the pressed element automatically. It's a recommendation, not a requirement.
- **Firefox's support is unclear.** Its test data marks some touch-capture tests as expected failures, and I couldn't confirm that its automatic touch capture works in all cases.
- **The grid really needs capture.** Every drag leaves the cell it started on. When you drag up toward the top edge to auto-scroll, your finger ends up over the sticky day header, which is outside the rows container. Without capture, the rows would stop receiving `pointermove` and `pointerup`. Auto-scroll would stall and a drag could be left unfinished.
- **Explicit capture removes that dependency,** and it matches what mouse already does (capture to the rows).
- **The try/catch matters:** `setPointerCapture` throws if the pointer has already ended. Automatic capture on the cell still exists as a backup.

It costs 7 lines. Everything else from the smaller version is in place: no `startDrag`, no `commitDrag`, no `DragStart`, and no `pointerYRef` update during the hold.

## 1. Diff and line counts

| File | Added / removed | Ignoring whitespace |
|---|---|---|
| `hooks/useWeeklyGridDrag.ts` | +118 / −30 (201 → 289 lines) | **+104 / −16** |
| `components/WeeklyAvailabilityGrid.tsx` | +3 / −2 | |
| `components/WeeklyAvailabilityGrid.test.tsx` | +5 / −4 | |

The previous version was +140 / −31. My earlier estimate of "+70 / −8" was too low, for three reasons:
- `onPointerUp` now takes the event, so the 13 unchanged commit lines were re-indented. They show as removed and added, but `git diff -w` shows them as unchanged.
- The explicit capture is 7 lines.
- I kept the explanatory comments.

The mouse and pen code is the original lines unchanged, except that the drag object now has `pointerId` and is created a few lines higher up.

All existing drag tests still pass unchanged: click toggle, deselect, same-day only, clamping, cancel, right-click ignored, read-only, and auto-scroll. They all use the mouse. **The touch path still has no unit tests**, as agreed for the proof of concept.

## 3. Biome

- **Formatting:** clean. I checked copies of the files with Windows line endings removed. Your `core.autocrlf=true` is the only reason a plain `biome check` reports formatting errors on these files.
- **1 warning:** `noExcessiveLinesPerFunction` on `useWeeklyGridDrag`. The hook is now over the 100-line limit (the previous version was 145 lines).
- **20 info-level notes** from experimental `nursery` rules (`useExplicitType`, `noTernary`), most of which were already there. Two are new, at lines 255 and 259: the arrow functions inside the `useEffect`. They follow the same pattern as the existing code (for example the cleanup in `useEdgeAutoScroll`).

## 4. TypeScript

I ran `tsc --noEmit` on `packages/features`. **There are no errors in any changed file, and none in `WeeklyAvailabilityGrid`.** The package already has 89 errors elsewhere, such as `business-days-plugin.ts` and `TimezoneSelectComponent.tsx`. One of them is in `schedules/components/ScheduleComponent.tsx` (a missing `@calcom/atoms` module). That file has no changes against `main`, so the error was already there.

## 5. Remaining browser risks

1. **Android Chrome long press (highest risk):** Chrome's own long-press action fires `contextmenu` around 400–500ms, after our drag has started. The menu is blocked, but there's no evidence either way on whether Chrome also fires `pointercancel`. **[device]**
2. **Mixing pointer and touch events:** the spec doesn't define how they interact, so blocking `touchmove` to stop the browser's scroll is a common approach, not a guaranteed one. Check B in DevTools is the first real test. **[DevTools → device]**
3. **Pen:** `touch-pan-y` may let the browser scroll during a vertical pen drag, which fires `pointercancel` and drops the drag. That only stays safe if the browser also sends touch events for the pen. DevTools can't emulate a pen. **[iPad with Pencil or Windows pen]**
4. **Windows touchscreen and desktop Firefox:** if a browser doesn't send touch events there, scrolling can't be blocked, so the long-press drag gets cancelled. The selection doesn't change, so it fails safely. **[device]**
5. **iOS Safari:** the callout and text-selection magnifier during the hold. **[iPhone]**
6. **Taps that stop a scroll:** with no scroll guard, tapping to stop a moving scroll can toggle a cell. This is expected for now.
7. **Capture:** automatic capture is no longer something we rely on. If the explicit call fails, behavior falls back to whatever automatic capture the browser does.

For manual testing, the DevTools steps from my previous message still apply (checks A–I). Check B and a top-edge auto-scroll drag are the most important now, because the top-edge drag moves your finger over the sticky header. Remember to temporarily add `availabilityView="grid"` in `schedule-view.tsx` and undo it with `git restore` afterwards.

```text
/**
 * jsdom does not implement PointerEvent, so `fireEvent.pointerDown` etc. fall back to a plain Event
 * without `pointerId`, `pointerType` or `isPrimary`. This minimal stand-in fills those in for tests.
 */
export function installPointerEventPolyfill(): void {
  if (typeof window.PointerEvent !== "undefined") return;

  class PointerEventPolyfill extends MouseEvent {
    pointerId: number;
    pointerType: string;
    isPrimary: boolean;

    constructor(type: string, init: PointerEventInit = {}) {
      super(type, init);
      this.pointerId = init.pointerId ?? 1;
      this.pointerType = init.pointerType ?? "mouse";
      this.isPrimary = init.isPrimary ?? true;
    }
  }

  Object.defineProperty(window, "PointerEvent", { value: PointerEventPolyfill, configurable: true });
}
```
</details></tool-use>

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-29 04:09:16Z)**_

I confirmed the bug and fixed it. A second finger now cancels the long-press drag, and nothing gets saved. Nothing is committed or pushed.

**Cause:** when a second finger touched down, `onPointerDown` only cancelled a hold that was still in its 350ms wait. Once the hold had finished and the drag had started, the second finger was ignored, so your first finger kept selecting.

**Fix** (`packages/features/schedules/hooks/useWeeklyGridDrag.ts`, around line 150):
```ts
if (!event.isPrimary || pendingTouchHoldRef.current || dragRef.current) {
  // A second contact means a pinch or multi-touch gesture, so the hold or drag the first one
  // started is abandoned rather than committed
  cancelTouchHold();
  endDrag();
  return;
}
```
- The selection preview goes back to how it was before the drag, and nothing is saved.
- After that, moving the first finger selects nothing, and lifting it saves nothing.
- The check also covers any second contact while a hold or drag is active, not just a second finger. For example, a finger touching down during a pen or mouse drag also cancels that drag. A mouse drag on its own is unaffected, since one mouse can't press down twice.

**Tests** (a new `touch` block in `useWeeklyGridDrag.test.tsx`, using fake timers):
1. **Second finger after the hold:** hold 350ms, drag to slot 40 and confirm the preview shows, then a second finger touches down. The preview reverts, moving the first finger selects nothing, and lifting both saves nothing.
2. **Second finger during the hold:** a second finger at 250ms means the drag never starts. Lifting the first finger doesn't toggle a slot either.

**Checks:**
- **Tests:** all schedules tests pass (241 passed, 4 skipped).
- **The test catches the bug:** with the old check put back temporarily, the "second finger after the hold" test failed. I then restored the fix.
- **Biome:** no new warnings. The only one left in the hook is the same over-length-function warning from before.

**One limitation:** the hook only sees a second finger if it lands on the grid's time slots. A finger on the day headers or elsewhere on the page won't cancel the drag. Catching those would need a page-wide listener, which I didn't add since you asked to hold off on page-wide listeners for now.

**To retest on your laptop:**
1. Long-press an empty slot and drag down a little.
2. Add a second finger on the grid. The highlight should disappear.
3. Keep moving the first finger. Nothing should be selected, though the grid may scroll.
4. Lift both fingers. Nothing should be saved.

Reminder: undo the temporary grid-view change before you commit with `git restore "apps/web/modules/availability/[schedule]/schedule-view.tsx"`.
